page_title: AmpereOne at Hot Chips 2024: Maximizing Density

sources.entry: AmpereOne at Hot Chips 2024: Maximizing Density - Puts vendor slides beside measurements of the predictor, small instruction cache, private L2 and long memory latency.

summary.title: AmpereOne at Hot Chips 2024: Maximizing Density
summary.one_liner: A measured look at Ampere's custom AmpereOne server core, covering its small 16 KB instruction cache, 8-table TAGE predictor, large private 2 MB L2, and density-first design tradeoffs compared with Zen 4, Neoverse V2 and Crestmont.
keywords: how to tell if a cpu design is dense
takeaways: AmpereOne uses an in-house core with a 16 KB L1 instruction cache, a 10 cycle mispredict recovery time, and an 8-table TAGE branch predictor.
The core favors density and consistency over peak performance: it has no SMT, a 64 KB 4-way L1D, and a 2 MB private L2 with about 11 cycle latency.
Measured per-core results show it is competitive with Skylake clock-for-clock on 7-Zip but trails Crestmont and higher-clocked designs on libx264 because of its weaker FP/vector side.
The chiplet design uses TSMC 5 nm for the compute die and 7 nm for IO, with 8x9 mesh, memory tagging, and adaptive traffic management.
summary.summary: Chips and Cheese examines Ampere's AmpereOne server CPU, presented at Hot Chips 2024, by pairing Ampere's slide claims with the author's microbenchmarks run on an Oracle Cloud instance capped at 3 GHz. The article walks through the frontend (branch prediction, BTB levels, small L1i, decode and fusion), the backend (eight schedulers, 12 execution pipes, FP scheduler depth), load/store behavior, the private L2, and the chiplet and mesh system layout. Results are compared against AMD Zen 4, Neoverse V2, Intel Crestmont and Nvidia Grace where relevant. The author concludes the core trades peak performance for density and consistent behavior.
